readings.c1s3:
¶
'''unsparingness''' (un-spãr′ing-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unsparing.

'''unspatial''' (un-spā′shal), ''a.'' Not spatial; not occupying space; having no extension. Also ''unspacial.''

'''unspatiality''' (un-spā-shi-al′i-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unspatial. Also ''unspaciality.''

'''unspeak''' (un-spēk′), ''v. t.'' To recant; retract, as what has been spoken; unsay. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 123.

'''unspeakable''' (un-spē′ka̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Incapable of being spoken or uttered; unutterable; ineffable; inexpressible.
{{smaller block|Joy ''unspeakable'' and full of glory. {{right|1 Pet. i. 8.}}
<poem>The day ''unspeakable'' draws nigh,
When bathed in unknown flame all things shall lie.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 217.}}}}
'''2.''' Extreme; extremely bad: as, an ''unspeakable'' fool; an ''unspeakable'' play. [Colloq.]

'''unspeakably''' (un-spē′ka̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a manner or degree that cannot be expressed; inexpressibly; unutterably. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 54.

'''unspeaking''' (un-spē′king), ''a.'' Without the power or gift of speech or utterance. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 5. 178.

'''unspecified''' (un-spes′i-fīd), ''a.'' Not specified; not specifically mentioned. ''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., vii. 1.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unsped†''' (un-sped′), ''a.'' Not performed; not despatched. ''Garth,'' tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xiv.

'''unspeed†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''unsped,'' < AS. ''unspēd,'' unsuccess, misfortune, poverty, < ''un-,'' not, + ''spēd,'' success, prosperity: see ''un-''<sup>1</sup> and ''speed.''] Ill success; lack of prosperity.

'''unspeedful†''' (un-spēd′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unspedful;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''speedful.''] Unsuccessful; ineffective.
{{smaller block|Preyeres that ne mowen ne ben ''unspedful'' ne withoute effect.
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Boëthius, v. prose 6.}}}}

'''unspeedy''' (un-spē′di), ''a.'' Not speedy; slow. ''Sandys,'' Travailes (1652), p. 92.

'''unspell''' (un-spel′), ''v. t.'' To release from the power of a spell or enchantment; disenchant. ''Dryden.''

'''unspent''' (un-spent′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not spent: as, money ''unspent;'' not used or wasted: as, water in a cistern ''unspent.''—'''2.''' Not exhausted: as, strength or force ''unspent.''—'''3.''' Not having lost its force of motion: as, an ''unspent'' ball.

'''unsphere''' (un-sfēr′), ''v. t.'' To remove from a sphere.
{{smaller block|To ''unsphere'' the stars.
{{right|''Shak.,'' W. T., i. 2. 48.}}}}

'''unspied''' (un-spīd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not spied or narrowly searched; not explored. ''Milton,'' P. L., iv. 529.—'''2.''' Not espied or seen; not discovered.

'''unspike''' (un-spīk′), ''v. t.'' To remove a spike from, as from the vent of a cannon.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''unspilled, unspilt''' (un-spild′, -spilt′), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not spoiled; not marred. ''Tusser'', September’s Husbandry.—'''2.''' Not spilled; not shed: as, blood ''unspilt.'' ''Denham'', Cooper’s Hill.

'''unspin''' (un-spin′), ''v. t.'' To undo, as something that has been spun.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh, cruell fates! the which so soone
His vitall thred ''unsponne.''</poem>
{{right|Quoted in ''Holinshed’s Chron.'' (Hist. Scot.).}}}}

'''unspirit†''' (un-spir′it), ''v. t.'' To depress in spirits; dispirit; dishearten. ''Norris.''

'''unspiritual''' (un-spir′i-t̮ū-al), ''a.'' Not spiritual; carnal; worldly. ''Jer. Taylor'', Sermons, II. 1. {{smaller|='''Syn.''' See ''worldly.''}}

'''unspiritualize''' (un-spir′i-t̮ū-al-īz), ''v. t.'' To deprive of spirituality. ''South'', Sermons, VI. 262.

'''unspiritually''' (un-spir′i-t̮ū-al-i), ''adv.'' In an unspiritual manner; without spirituality.

'''unspleened''' (un-splēnd′), ''a.'' Devoid of spleen.
{{smaller block|Vouchsafe one ''unspleen’d'' chiding to my riot.
{{right|''Ford'', Lady’s Trial, ii. 4.}}}}

'''unspoil''' (un-spoil′), ''v. t.'' To undo or destroy the effect of spoiling or over-indulgence in; cure of being spoiled or over-indulged. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|“I am quite spoiled, I believe,” said Helen; “you must ''unspoil'' me, Esther.” ''Miss Edgeworth'', Helen, xliii.}}

'''unspoiled''' (un-spoild′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not spoiled; not corrupted; not ruined; not having lost its naturalness and simplicity: as, an ''unspoiled'' character.
{{smaller block|Bathurst! yet ''unspoil’d'' by wealth.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii. 226.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
2. Not despoiled or plundered; not pillaged. ''Dryden'', Æneid, x.

'''unspoken''' (un-spō′kn), ''a.'' Not spoken or uttered; hence, unconfessed.
{{smaller block|What to speak, . . . what to leave ''unspoken.'' {{right|''Bacon.''}}
These black weeds have sprung up out of a buried heart, to make manifest an ''unspoken'' crime.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, p. 160.}}}}

'''unspontaneous''' (un-spon-tā′nẹ̄-us), ''a.'' Not spontaneous; not voluntary; forced; artificial: as, ''unspontaneous'' laughter. ''Cowper'', Odyssey, xx.

'''unsportful''' (un-spōrt′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not sportful, gay, or merry; sad; uncheerful; melancholy. ''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. iv. 4.

'''unspotted''' (un-spot′ed), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not spotted or stained; free from spots. ''Emerson'', Misc., p. 41.—'''2.''' Free from moral stain; untainted with guilt; immaculate. Jas. i. 27.—'''3.''' Free from ceremonial uncleanness.
{{smaller block|By the sacrifice of an ''unspotted'' lambe.
{{right|''J. Udall'', On Mark ix.}}}}
'''4.''' Unblemished; faultless; pure; perfect.
{{smaller block|Cæsar’s Commentaries, . . . wherein is seene the ''unspotted'' proprietie of the Latin tongue.
{{right|''Ascham'', Scholemaster, p. 263. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''unspottedness''' (un-spot′ed-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unspotted. ''Feltham'', Resolves, ii. 3.

'''unsquared''' (un-skwãrd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not made square: as, ''unsquared'' timber.—'''2.''' Not properly formed or proportioned; irregular.
{{smaller block|<poem>When he speaks,
’Tis like a chime a-mending; with terms ''unsquared.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3. 159.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''unstack''' (un-stak′), ''v. t.'' To remove from a stack; undo from a stacked position: as, to ''unstack'' hay; to ''unstack'' guns.

'''unstaid''' (un-stād′), ''a.'' Not staid or steady; not settled in judgment; volatile; fickle: as, ''unstaid'' youth. ''Nashe'', Pierce Penilesse, p. 57.

'''unstaidness''' (un-stād′nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state or character of being unstaid.—'''2†.''' Uncertain or motion; unsteadiness.
{{smaller block|A kind of shaking ''unstaidness'' over all his body.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i.}}}}

'''unstained''' (un-stānd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not stained; not dyed.—'''2.''' Not polluted; not tarnished; not dishonored: as, an ''unstained'' character; ''unstained'' religion. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 1.

'''unstamped''' (un-stampt′), ''a.'' Not stamped or impressed; not having a stamp impressed or affixed: as, an ''unstamped'' deed, receipt, or letter.

'''unstanch, unstaunch''' (un-stȧnch′, -stänch′), ''a.'' Not stanch; not strong and tight. ''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 465.

'''unstanchable, unstaunchable''' (un-stȧn′cha-bl, -stän′cha-bl), ''a.'' [ME. ''unstaunchable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stanch''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.] '''1†.''' Inexhaustible; illimitable.
{{smaller block|Eternite that is ''unstaunchable'' and infynyt.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 7.}}}}
'''2.''' Not capable of being stanched, as a bleeding wound.

'''unstanched, unstaunched''' (un-stȧncht′, -stäncht′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unstaunched''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stanched, staunched''.] '''1.''' Not stanched; not stopped, as blood.—'''2.''' Unsatisfied; unsated.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unsoul|6647|unsteadfast}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''unsoul†''' (un-sōl′), ''v. t.'' To deprive of mind, soul, or understanding; deprive of spirit.
{{smaller block|Your sad appearance, should they thus behold you, Would half ''unsoul'' your army.
{{right|''Chapman'', Revenge for Honour, i. 2.}}
Thus bodies walk ''unsoul’d!'' ''Ford'', Love’s Sacrifice, i. 2.}}

'''unsound''' (un-sound′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unsownd.''] Not sound. {{smaller|(''a'') Not healthy; diseased; morbid; corrupt; rotten; decayed: as, an ''unsound'' body or mind; ''unsound'' teeth; ''unsound'' timber; ''unsound'' fruit. (''b'') Not solid, firm, strong, compact, or the like; not whole or entire: as, ''unsound'' ice. (''c'') Not founded on truth or correct principles; ill-founded; not valid; incorrect; erroneous; wrong; not orthodox: as, ''unsound'' reasoning or arguments; ''unsound'' doctrine or opinions. (''d'') Not sincere; not genuine or true; faithless; deceitful. ''Spenser'', F. Q., V. ii. 36. (''e''†) Not safe; injured.}}
{{smaller block|Than assembles fulle sone sevene score knyghtes, In sighte to thaire soverayne, that was ''unsownde'' levede.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4295.}}}}
'''Of unsound mind''', insane. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Defective, imperfect, impaired, infirm.}}

'''unsoundable''' (un-soun′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Not soundable; deep; profound; unfathomable. ''Leighton'', Com. on 1 Pet. ii.

'''unsoundly†''' (un-sound′li), ''adv.'' In an unsound manner.
{{smaller block|Discipline ''unsoundly'' taught.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, Pref., § 8.}}}}

'''unsoundness''' (un-sound′nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unsound, in any sense.
{{smaller block|The ''unsoundness'' of his own judgment.
{{right|''Milton'', Ans. to Eikon Basilike, § 7.}}}}

'''unspar''' (un-spär′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unsperren'', ''unsperen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''spar''<sup>1</sup>.] To withdraw or remove the spars or bars of; unbolt; unfasten; open. {{smaller block|Loke if the gate be ''unspered''. ''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 2656.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Forty yeomen tall . . .
The lofty palisade ''unsparred'',
And let the drawbridge fall.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, i. 4.}}}}

'''unspared''' (un-spãrd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not spared; not saved for future use; not treated with mildness; not saved from destruction, ruin, death, or the like. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 606.—'''2†.''' Indispensable; not to be spared.
{{smaller block|No physician then cures of himself, no more than the hand feeds the mouth. The meat doth the one, the medicine doth the other; though the physician and the hand be ''unspared'' instruments to their several purposes.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 381.}}}}

'''unsparely†''' (un-spãr′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unsparely'', ''unsparliche'' (= Icel. ''ūsparliga''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''sparely''.] Not sparely; unsparingly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Chefly thay asken
Spycez, that ''vn-sparely'' men speded hom to bryng,
& the wynne-lych wyne ther-with vche tyme.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 979.}}}}

'''unsparing''' (un-spãr′ing), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not sparing; liberal; profuse; abundant: as, the ''unsparing'' use of money.
{{smaller block|Heaps with ''unsparing'' hand. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 344.}}
'''2.''' Not merciful; unmerciful: as, ''unsparing'' publicity.
{{smaller block|The ''unsparing'' sword of justice.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, Pref.}}}}

'''unsparingly''' (un-spãr′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unsparing manner; profusely; also, mercilessly.
{{smaller block|The birch rod had to be ''unsparingly'' applied before he could be induced to enter the school-room.
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LXVI. 481.}}}}

'''unsparingness''' (un-spãr′ing-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unsparing.

'''unspatial''' (un-spā′shal), ''a.'' Not spatial; not occupying space; having no extension. Also ''unspacial.''

'''unspatiality''' (un-spā-shi-al′i-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unspatial. Also ''unspaciality.''

'''unspeak''' (un-spēk′), ''v. t.'' To recant; retract, as what has been spoken; unsay. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 123.

{{smaller block|Joy ''unspeakable'' and full of glory. {{right|1 Pet. i. 8.}}
<poem>The day ''unspeakable'' draws nigh,
When bathed in unknown flame all things shall lie.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 217.}}}}
'''2.''' Extreme; extremely bad: as, an ''unspeakable'' fool; an ''unspeakable'' play. [Colloq.]

'''unspeakably''' (un-spē′ka̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a manner or degree that cannot be expressed; inexpressibly; unutterably. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 54.

'''unspeaking''' (un-spē′king), ''a.'' Without the power or gift of speech or utterance. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 5. 178.

'''unsped†''' (un-sped′), ''a.'' Not performed; not despatched. ''Garth,'' tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xiv.

'''unspeed†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''unsped,'' < AS. ''unspēd,'' unsuccess, misfortune, poverty, < ''un-,'' not, + ''spēd,'' success, prosperity: see ''un-''<sup>1</sup> and ''speed.''] Ill success; lack of prosperity.

{{smaller block|Preyeres that ne mowen ne ben ''unspedful'' ne withoute effect.
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Boëthius, v. prose 6.}}}}

'''unspiritual''' (un-spir′i-t̮ū-al), ''a.'' Not spiritual; carnal; worldly. ''Jer. Taylor'', Sermons, II. 1. {{smaller|='''Syn.''' See ''worldly.''}}

'''unspiritualize''' (un-spir′i-t̮ū-al-īz), ''v. t.'' To deprive of spirituality. ''South'', Sermons, VI. 262.

'''unspiritually''' (un-spir′i-t̮ū-al-i), ''adv.'' In an unspiritual manner; without spirituality.

{{smaller block|Vouchsafe one ''unspleen’d'' chiding to my riot.

{{smaller block|“I am quite spoiled, I believe,” said Helen; “you must ''unspoil'' me, Esther.” ''Miss Edgeworth'', Helen, xliii.}}

'''unspoiled''' (un-spoild′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not spoiled; not corrupted; not ruined; not having lost its naturalness and simplicity: as, an ''unspoiled'' character.
{{smaller block|Bathurst! yet ''unspoil’d'' by wealth.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii. 226.}}}} 2. Not despoiled or plundered; not pillaged. ''Dryden'', Æneid, x.

'''unspoken''' (un-spō′kn), ''a.'' Not spoken or uttered; hence, unconfessed.

{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, p. 160.}}}}

<poem>I should feare my form,
Lest ought I offer’d were ''unsquard'' or warp’d.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Marston'', What you Will, Ind.}}}}

'''unsquire''' (un-skwīr′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''squire''<sup>1</sup>.] To divest of the title or privileges of an esquire; degrade from the rank of squire. ''Swift'', Letters to the King-at-arms. [Rare.]

'''unstability''' (un-stạ̄-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' Instability. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The ''unstability'' of such an association is, however, beginning to be understood.
{{right|''Science'', VIII. 401.}}}}

'''unstable<sup>1</sup>''' (un-stā′bl), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''stable''<sup>1</sup>.] To make no longer a stable or filthy abode. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Our hearts be ''unstabled'' of these bestial lusts.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 326.}}}}

'''unstable<sup>2</sup>''' (un-stā′bl), ''a.'' [ME. ''unstable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stable''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Not stable; not fixed.
{{smaller block|It is true of a social aggregate, as of every other aggregate, that the state of homogeneity is an ''unstable'' state; and that, where there is already some heterogeneity, the tendency is towards greater heterogeneity.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 454.}}}}
'''2.''' Not steady; inconstant; irresolute; wavering.
{{smaller block|''Unstable'' as water, thou shalt not excel [have the excellency, R. V.].
{{right|Gen. xlix. 4.}}}}
'''Unstable equilibrium.''' {{smaller|See ''equilibrium'', 1.}}

'''unstabled''' (un-stā′bld), ''a.'' Not put up in a stable.
{{smaller block|Behold the branchless tree, the ''unstabled'' Rosinante!
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Villette, xxxix.}}}}

'''unstableness''' (un-stā′bl-nes), ''n.'' Instability. ''Sir M. Hale'', On Eccles. xii. 1.

'''unstack''' (un-stak′), ''v. t.'' To remove from a stack; undo from a stacked position: as, to ''unstack'' hay; to ''unstack'' guns.

'''unstanch, unstaunch''' (un-stȧnch′, -stänch′), ''a.'' Not stanch; not strong and tight. ''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 465.

'''unstanchable, unstaunchable''' (un-stȧn′cha-bl, -stän′cha-bl), ''a.'' [ME. ''unstaunchable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stanch''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.] '''1†.''' Inexhaustible; illimitable.
{{smaller block|Eternite that is ''unstaunchable'' and infynyt.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 7.}}}}
'''2.''' Not capable of being stanched, as a bleeding wound.

'''unstanched, unstaunched''' (un-stȧncht′, -stäncht′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unstaunched''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stanched, staunched''.] '''1.''' Not stanched; not stopped, as blood.—'''2.''' Unsatisfied; unsated. {{smaller block|Rychesse may nat restreyne avarice ''unstaunched.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Stifle the villain whose ''unstanched'' thirst
York and young Rutland could not satisfy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 6. 83.}}}}
'''3.''' Not made stauch or tight.
{{smaller block|The elements . . . came pouring from ''unstanchea'' roofs. {{right|''H. Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. 378. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unstarch''' (un-stärch′), ''v. t.'' To take the starch or stiffening from; hence, to free from stiffness, reserve, formality, pride, haughtiness, or the like; relax.
{{smaller block|<poem>One that weighs
His breath between his teeth, and dares not smile
Beyond a point, for fear t’ ''unstarch'' his look.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iii. 2.}}}}

'''unstate''' (un-stāt′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To deprive of state or dignity. ''Shak.'', Lear, i. 2. 108.—'''2.''' To deprive of statehood; cause to cease to be a state. ''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 23.

'''unstatutable''' (un-stat′ū-tạ-bl), ''a.'' Contrary to statute; not warranted by statute. ''Swift'', On the Power of the Bishops.

'''unstatutably''' (un-stat′ū-tạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unstatutable manner; without warrant of statute. ''Encyc. Brit.'', V. 228.

'''unsteadfast, unstedfast''' (un-sted′fȧst), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unstedfast, unstedefast''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''steadfast.''] '''1.''' Not steadfast; not firmly fixed or established.
{{smaller block|<poem>A fooles displeasure to a wyse man is found profytable;
For his good will is ''vnstedfast.''</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 95.}}}}
'''2.''' Not firmly adhering to a purpose; inconstant; irresolute.—'''3.''' Insecure; unsafe. ''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 3. 193.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
